recorded: 2026-09-28, gfx1151 Strix Halo (zbook), Gemma 4 26B-A4B UD-Q4_K_XL, Q5_1 staged grouped-prefill
candidate: software-pipeline the Q5_1 staged grouped-prefill kernel's packed byte loads, so chunk c+1's two global loads are issued before chunk c's arithmetic instead of in front of it. The inner loop's critical path runs load -> nibble select -> or with the staged qh bit -> cvt -> multiply-add -> fused multiply-add, and the chunk loop carries no unroll, so the intent was to take the load latency off that path.
reason: The change is bit-identical at all three geometries and is not faster. It also shows why: it adds more instructions than the latency it hides.

mechanism.bit_exactness: verified by A/B against the kernel's own prior behaviour on the same kernel, not against another kernel: run the pipelined kernel on seeded inputs, git stash the change, rebuild, run the original on identical inputs, compare bf16 output bits.
mechanism.why_gemma4_geometry_matters: chunks = ceil(704/256) = 3, an odd count, so the pipeline's last-iteration guard runs at a different point in the rotation than at the 11-chunk Qwen4Exp geometry. Both are covered.

cost.reading: the prefetch's addressing arithmetic is computed twice per chunk instead of once (next_chunk * SUBS + sub, the row pointer, the bound test) and the rotation adds a copy, which is where the 406 extra VALU per wave comes from.

performance.platform: zbook, Strix Halo, Radeon 8060S Graphics, gfx1151, 125 GiB unified memory, HIPENGINE_HIP_ARCH=gfx1151
performance.protocol: paired, back to back in one session on one device, one warm-up then three timed 512-token forwards through scripts.gemma4_campaign_bench._public_wall
performance.delta: +0.8% slower, inside the 2% run-to-run spread of either arm
performance.reading: neutral to slightly negative. Not a win, and not evidence of a loss either.

what_this_establishes: The packed-load latency is not what the kernel is waiting on. This is the third refutation in this family, after rowbatch8 (1.31x slower) and shared-memory staging (1.13x slower), and it is the first that was aimed at latency rather than instruction count.

Adding 9.4% more VALU instructions per wave cost 0.8% of the time, so VALU issue is not the binding resource either. That is a useful asymmetry against the earlier probe, which removed the dequant and its loads and recovered 20%: removing that work helps far more than its instruction count predicts, while adding instruction count elsewhere barely registers.

The compiler was already scheduling this loop. The chunk loop is a simple counted loop and LLVM's scheduler software-pipelines it; the manual rotation duplicated the address arithmetic without shortening any dependency.

next_candidate.hypothesis: one pipeline stage is not deep enough. The load for chunk c+1 is issued ~92 instructions per thread before it is used, which is roughly 92 issue cycles against a latency that is a few hundred cycles even on an L2 hit. A two- or three-deep pipeline would put the load further ahead.
next_candidate.why_it_is_not_obvious: the same measurement says the extra registers and addressing cost real time, and a deeper pipeline multiplies both. VGPR went 88 -> 96 for one stage, and the kernel is resident at 23 of 32 waves, so there is headroom before occupancy drops but not a lot.
next_candidate.cheaper_first_step: if the address arithmetic is what made this neutral, hoisting the per-chunk row pointer and sub index out of the prefetch is a strictly cheaper version of the same idea and is not yet measured.

limits: One box, one artifact, one session. Both arms ran in one session but in two processes, so the comparison carries process-to-process drift; the incumbent's 1.897 s mean here against its recorded 1.880 s mean in the previous unit is that drift, about 1%.
No counter profile was taken of the incumbent in the same session, so the 4304 VALU per wave it is compared against is the previous unit's reading rather than a paired one.
The prefill-only harness was used; decode was not re-measured because the change is in a prefill kernel and the timing was not a win.

provenance.reverted: the kernel file was restored byte for byte (md5 matched the pre-change copy)
